title: Cascading meteors over Kitt Peak
caption: Geminid meteors and the Milky Way above the McMath-Pierce Solar Telescope, Kitt Peak, Arizona
celestial: Photograph taken at Kitt Peak National Observatory, Arizona

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Bright streaks of the Geminid meteor shower rain down over the McMath-Pierce Solar Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory, with the Milky Way rising high overhead.

The Geminids come every December, when Earth passes through a trail of debris left by the asteroid 3200 Phaethon. As the bits of debris hit the atmosphere, they burn up in bright flashes. Most major meteor showers come from comets, and the Geminids are one of only two that don’t.

Asteroids are a theme on this mountain. Two of Kitt Peak’s telescopes, the University of Arizona’s 0.9-meter and 1.8-meter Spacewatch telescopes, are used to study them, tracking small Solar System bodies to learn how the Solar System has changed over time. The photographer, Rob Sparks, is one of NOIRLab’s Audiovisual Ambassadors.

understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, and this picture likely gathers meteors that flashed at different moments; the source doesn’t say how it was made.

explore: A meteor shower seems to come from one point in the sky, called its radiant. For the Geminids that point is in the constellation Gemini, which is how the shower got its name.
alt: Many bright meteor streaks across a starry sky above a tall, angular white telescope, with the Milky Way rising behind.
